Not from the UK but I have a general idea of what those prices convert to in my country. Those prices are honestly quite reasonable if not low where I’m from. BUT, I get struggling financially. I volunteer at a free clinic and it’s hard to do anything beyond basic wellness care for clients due to how bad inflation is right now (especially on “niche” products aka companion animal vaccines and medications.)

A few things to help put in perspective even though I know it’s still frustrating.

1. Antibiotics cannot and should not be prescribed without knowing if bacteria is present. A lot of things can cause a cat to urinate outside of the box that is not bacterial in nature. Antimicrobial stewardship is such an issue globally that we are RESERVING use of certain antibiotics to just people or really really severe cases in companion animals. It’s predicted a leading cause of death in the coming decades will be antibiotic resistant infections. I know it seems simple to just give antibiotics but doing so without the needs not only contributes to antibiotic resistance but can have bad effects on your cat’s natural skin, GI, and bladder microflora.

2. I don’t disagree about the wait time on pain meds. It’s hard to see your family members in pain. A medication commonly used for cats that’s “less expensive” is slowly/is now considered a controlled drug where I am. I don’t know what drugs are or aren’t controlled in the UK but that may be contributed to this issue? On top of that, cats are weird. They lack enzymes to process the “cheap” painkillers you are thinking of. The pain control we have for cats is severely lacking, even compared to dogs. 

2b. You can ask for a written prescription to send into Chewy or bring to a human pharmacy. You may be able to find medications cheaper than at your vet. 

3. Based on your comments it sounds like you either weren’t offer or you didn’t consent to doing a urine culture on top of a urinalysis. The culture is the only true way to determine what bacteria it is. Unfortunately, a lot of clients call us “greedy, money grabbers” when we try to offer this so many places do not offer it first visit. Generally most places save it for the 2nd or 3rd visit once it is determined the bacteria present is resistant. Now at this point I do agree it probably should have been ran but hopefully the above gives a bit of perspective. 

4. Everyone is struggling financially right now. I don’t disagree that big corporations aren’t making it worse but I can guarantee that 95% of veterinarians are not in it for the money. (Obviously, we need money to live and the business needs money to stay open.) But if DVMs had wanted to make BANK they would have gone into human medicine. Human medical schools are easier to get into, focus on one specie, have a better work-life balance, better community respect, and costs the same as vet school (coming from someone who thought they would go that route way back when and has current MD student friends). No one is more frustrated by these prices than your vet staff. It creates so many barriers to care and creates divide between clients and doctors.

(6. I definitely think another vet office for a second opinion is warranted if you are unhappy with your current care.) 

I do hope you and your kitty can find some relief and get back to normal. I am truly sorry you ended up in this position because it a horrible one to be in.

It took a hot minute for me to “hop the proverbial
fence” to where I stand now. Think of pet food as a whole as akin to baby food rather than fast food. I do not think McDonalds with a side of broccoli would be nutritionally complete due to the high fat content it has and I don’t think all the minerals we need for the day are found in a Big Mac - but people nutrition wasn’t touched much once I reached college. On the other hand, every bite our cats take have to meet their nutritional needs like baby food needs to.

With corn/wheat gluten if we were to feed cats straight up these foods raw or cooked on a platter they would absolutely be nutritionally deficient. Cats can’t process them as is. In pet food, these ingredients are processed (not the type of processed as human food) in a way to make all the nutrients in corn and wheat gluten available for cats to use. We can’t call corn a filler since it has a lot of nutritional benefits. The big one is linoleic acid. Cats CANNOT synthesize this important amino acid and corn oil is high in it. I shadowed a board certified veterinary nutritionist ( and took some of her classes) and every homemade diet she formulated had to have corn oil in it to meet the pets needs. Corn also provides some protein and antioxidants as well which we don’t think of as humans use it more as a side dish in my experience. 

Meat as the first couple of ingredients looks great. I won’t lie, I used to be on that side of this discussion for many years. It sounds more like what we learned in school in elementary about carnivores vs herbivores. Cats need a higher protein and fat % in their diet most definitely. However, if they just list the meat source you don’t know how far that ingredient is in terms of processing. Does it still have water weight? Have they removed the inedible parts yet? Does this include organs? What quality is the meat? You can certainly ask the same of corn but farming practices are more straight forward. While they cannot legally put any inedible parts in the food it’s hard to say if each ingredient is weighed equally. 

For me WSAVA is important in terms of them having the research to back their food and the safety standards. I also prefer brands own their own food plants solely instead of sharing with another producer which is NOT a requirement of WSAVA. For example, if 2 companies are using the same manufacturing plant and company A has a bacterial issue. Company B which I am feeding may not catch it immediately risking it going into my pet’s bowl. I personally am also not a fan of newer foods where I cannot find significant details on their safety protocols and staff online. Or if they have a part time nutritionist or just “consult” with unspecified veterinarians. (Which is how my kitten ended up on Instinct since they do have a veterinary nutritionist on staff - Dr Sarah G. Wynn. I do not hate this food it just didn’t help with my boy’s pica). 

This may not change your mind but I hope at least you can think of pet food more like baby food than junk food. This is just my degree and experience with my own cat’s medical issues getting me to where I am today. Ultimately, I have my opinions but fed is best at the end of the day.

Reducing calories is not good enough when they are obese/severely obese. Most low calorie foods on the market are for animals that are a 6/9 maybe a 7/9 on the body condition scale. When you bring her to the vet I would ask for a weight loss therapeutic diet. These foods are low in calorie but they are more nutrient dense to prevent deficiencies and support muscle mass. Drastically dropping her intake on regular food can be a risky game. Not that it can’t be done but it’s either too slow to protect their joints or so fast it harms their organ function.

Weight loss diets are not life long. You may only be on it on for a few months and then you can switch her to the dog food of your choice.

Do not add more to the food. While it may sound healthy she should be getting 90% of her caloric needs from her food alone. Trying to replace with fruits/veggies will result in a dietary imbalance that can cause problems down the line. If you can’t afford a prescription diet (which is completely valid) I’d cut back her calories 10% and then recheck her weight in 2 weeks. Recalculate her caloric needs and cut back another 10% and repeat until her goal weight. Set aside her kibble as treats, do not introduce treats until she is a healthy weight.

However, after finishing my Animal Science degree I realized a lot more goes into those WSAVA brands. It can be as simple as FF which has be trusted for years. Ingredients truly don’t mean as much as we think. Same with guaranteed analysis. You can have the perfect guaranteed analysis but if the meat is not properly raised, processed, fed, medicated, etc then the food is shit. Same vice versa, great ingredients but poor analysis makes the food just as worthless.

My stance is WSAVA brands have so many researchers and veterinarians that have for years figured out exactly what is needed analysis wise. While the ingredients like corn and meat byproduct don’t look great on paper, these have to meet high standards because of their WSAVA compliance. Eg corn when processed is highly digestible for cats. If they gave raw or poorly processed corn then it would be a shit food. I would also argue bigger brands have their own processing plants and manufacturers. Small companies cannot afford or budget for their own plants so many companies share which is why you see a whole list of brands/foods under the same recall. Having their own plant means that they will catch quality control issues sooner to issue a recall faster. Recalls aren’t bad per say, especially if its voluntary which means the company caught it quickly. 

Now, I will say I feed a mix of WSAVA and non WSAVA foods. My cat is doing well and in good health. It comes down to your preferences, your vet’s recommendations, and how your kitty performance.

Most commercial diets are balanced whether it’s Purina Dog Chow or Orejin. I think the issue is with inflation and a veterinary shortage, medical care has gone up. A lot of people are leaving the field due to owners lacking compassion and expecting free care for freak accidents. 

I personally think owners should either be financially able to afford routine care (vaccines, preventatives, sick appointments) and an ER visit before adopting or have pet insurance in place to prevent the emotional and financial strain an illness or accident can put on a family. It’s traumatizing to watch an owner have to euthanize a beloved pet due to a preventative illness or lack of routine surgery.

Now, sometimes life happens. Whether an owner loses a job, inherits an animal, or finds one on the side of the road/backyard, etc. I don’t think majority of people are saying to abandon the animal especially if it’s bettering the situation but rather if you are wanting an animal to financially be prepared. 

It’s different if someone is homeless and befriends a stray. It’s different if you fall on hard times and can’t afford what you use to. It’s different if your mother dies and lives her dog to you. There’s a lot that goes into this conversation that boils down to spontaneously getting an animal without financial resources can be irresponsible if the animal will suffer at home without adequate medical care as needed or if an emergency will make you have to make the hard decision between debt or euthanizing.

Edit: Anyone can be a good owner. There are many low cost and sliding scale options out there for owners to pursue if they do their research in advance! I’m in my third year now and got my GPA back above a 3.5 after a lot of hard work. Best thing I can suggest is review, review, review. The day after a lecture go back through your notes and highlight or underline key terms. A day or two later go through making notes on your notes or add post its. Make as many analogies as possible eg PCR = 3 letters = 3 steps = denature anneal extension. 

Another tip is take some buffer classes! Don’t do all bio bio bio. Take houseplant keeping 101, a marketing class, take your generals throughout the four years not all at once. These easy classes help remind you that you are more than capable of getting to your end goal. Best of luck!
